newsitem.title: GERMANY: WHO says eastern Europe breeding TB epidemics.
newsitem.headline: WHO says eastern Europe breeding TB epidemics.

text.p: The World Health Organisation (WHO) said on Wednesday eastern Europe had become one of the world's worst breeding grounds for tuberculosis and chastised the region for its "chaotic" treatment programmes.

Since the collapse of the Soviet bloc in 1991, the incidence of TB in some areas has more than doubled, due in part to crumbling health care infrastructure, the WHO said at the Berlin presentation of its 1997 TB report.

"A few years ago, the WHO was warning eastern Europe and Russia that the TB situation in parts of their countries could soon begin to rival that of Africa and Asia," said Richard Bumgarner, deputy director of the WHO's Global TB Programme.
"In fact it has now become much worse," he said. "Russia's prisoners, for instance, have TB case rates up to 10 times those in Zaire or India."

Bumgarner added that the Russian Federation had reported a 70 percent jump in TB infections in the general population since 1991 and an increase of more than 90 percent in TB-related deaths during that time.
"No other large country has recently experienced such a a skyrocketing increase in TB death rates," he said.

But a public health strategy called DOTS -- Directly Observed Treatment, Short course -- a demonstrably successful, low cost programme to wipe out even highly-resistant TB strains, could help ease the situation, Bumgarner said.
"If DOTS is put to work, both eastern and western Europe should be able to breathe easier."
DOTS involves training public health workers or community members to administer antibiotics until the patient is fully cured, and not just until symptoms disappear.
